title.en: The Chip Industry's Thirst: Semiconductors and Water Scarcity

source.note: No workbook sheet exists for this SDG 6 mission; authored from scratch per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md.

narrative_brief: Taiwan makes about 90% of the world's most advanced chips while also being one of the most water-stressed places on Earth. This talk traces that collision through TSMC's rising water use, the 2021 drought, genuine recycling and reclaiming progress, and the unresolved trade-off between industry and agriculture as droughts grow harder to predict.

A2.text: A tiny chip is smaller than your fingernail. But making one needs a huge amount of super clean water. Why does something so tiny need so much?
A2.authored_by: Claude + Gemini 3.1 Pro draft, fully rewritten by Claude for band compliance
A2.basis: New mission, no workbook source. Facts: Taiwan makes ~90% of the world's most advanced chips, led by TSMC (widely reported industry figure). TSMC total water use ~114 million m3 in 2023 rising to ~129 million m3 in 2024 (TSMC 2024 Sustainability Report, via secondary reporting). Science parks (Hsinchu, Central Taiwan, Southern Taiwan) draw a large, concentrated share of local water supply. 2021 drought: government ordered tech sector to cut water use by up to 20%; TSMC trucked in water (NPR/KPBS Apr 2023; multiple sources). TSMC process water recycling rate reached 90.3% in 2023 (TSMC sustainability report / Semiwiki summary). TSMC Tainan-area fabs used ~19.65 million m3 of reclaimed water in 2024, cutting tap-water use there by ~31% (TSMC 2024 report). Reclaimed-water plants operate in Tainan Science Park (e.g. Anping Reclaimed Water Plant). TSMC has pledged to be 'water positive' by 2030 (company target, not yet achieved). Desalination expanding as backup supply (Hsinchu desal plant). 2021 drought: >74,000 hectares of farmland left fallow, about the size of New York City (NPR/KPBS; Earth.org). Agriculture uses >70% of Taiwan's water but <2% of GDP (Earth.org; multiple sources). Register per docs/plans/new-mission-playbook.md. House rule followed: 'Silicon Shield' never used (per lint rule, this is a cross-strait deterrence term, not an industry nickname).
